title: Why “Handholding” Is Bad Classroom Management https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2021/08/27/why-handholding-is-bad-classroom-management/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin distinguishes true classroom management from what he calls 'handholding' — constant narration, correction, guidance, and praise that shepherds students through every step of a task. Though widely mistaken for good management because it keeps a lid on disorder, he argues handholding causes five specific harms: it strips students of purpose by removing their independent decision-making; it infantilizes them by signaling distrust in their competence; it produces learned helplessness as students disengage and rely on constant reteaching; it induces boredom by removing the freedom to try, succeed, or fail; and it breeds resentment, comparing the experience to an over-talkative sports announcer or tour guide ruining an otherwise enjoyable experience. His alternative is straightforward: teach expectations in detailed fashion, check thoroughly for understanding, then fully shift responsibility to students to execute independently while the teacher observes from a distance, which he argues produces happier, more mature, and more purpose-driven students.
points: 'Handholding' — constant narration, correction, and guidance during tasks — is widely mistaken for good classroom management but actually causes significant harm.
Handholding strips students of purpose and intrinsic motivation by removing their independent decision-making.
It produces learned helplessness, as students disengage mentally and require constant reteaching and reminding to do anything.
It breeds resentment, comparable to an over-talkative sports announcer or tour guide ruining an experience through constant chatter.
The alternative is to teach expectations in detail, check thoroughly for understanding, then fully shift responsibility to students while observing from a distance.
quotes: This is handholding—which is a gross misunderstanding of effective classroom management. It’s also terrible for students.

When students aren’t free to follow directions and pursue objectives without your frequent input, they turn their brains off. Their very purpose, which is the driving force behind intrinsic motivation, is ripped from their hands.
When you do for students what they can do for themselves, you communicate loud and clear that they can’t .
And when it’s time to get to work on their own, they require reteaching, restating, reminding, and mollycoddling.
This is how students feel all day with a handholding teacher. They become so stifled and defeated and tired of being steered and baby-talked that they become resentful.

It’s to teach what you want in a highly detailed way, check thoroughly for understanding, and then shift responsibility in toto over to your students to do the work, perform the routine, meet in groups, solve for x, participate in discussions, etc, etc, etc.
